newsitem.title: TURKEY: More than 100 dead in Turkey's Kurd rebel fight.
newsitem.headline: More than 100 dead in Turkey's Kurd rebel fight.

text.p: More than 100 people have died in two days of fighting between Turkish troops and Kurdish guerrillas that has spilled just across the border into northern Iraq, security officials said on Tuesday.
A high-ranking security official said troops had entered Iraqi territory in pinprick raids but had later withdrawn.

"Forces are established on the border to block all the crossing points into Turkey. From time to time they may cross just into Iraq but only to hit specific targets and come back again," he told Reuters. "It is not anything long term."
Turkey regularly sends its forces on anti-rebel incursions into northern Iraq, controlled by Iraqi Kurdish groups.
Security officials said 68 Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) rebels died in the province of Hakkari, near the Iraqi border, after the guerrillas launched a rocket attack on Monday night.

A further 25 PKK fighters were killed in separate fighting in the southeastern province of Diyarbakir. Eleven troops and one member of an anti-rebel Kurdish militia also died in the clashes, the officials said.
No independent confirmation of the death toll was available.

Tens of thousands of troops have been building up near the mountainous border with Iraq in recent weeks in preparation for a round of annual spring clashes with the PKK, which has bases on both sides of the border.
More than 22,000 people have died in 12 years of conflict between troops and the PKK, fighting for Kurdish self rule in southeast Turkey.
The state-run Anatolian news agency said the recent fighting had been intense.

"It has been established through long-range observation and listening to (PKK) wireless communications that the terrorists threw the bodies of their dead into the Zab river. They loaded their wounded on to donkeys and ran way," it said.
Rebel leader Abdullah Ocalan renewed a call at the weekend to Turkish authorities for dialogue on bringing the conflict to an end.
"We are ready for dialogue, we have alternatives. There must at last be a Turkish and Kurdish political solution," Ocalan said by telephone in a MED TV programme broadcast on Sunday evening.
Turkey has rejected frequent similar calls in the past by Ocalan, who Ankara says is based in Damascus or the Syrian-controlled Bekaa Valley in Lebanon.
